findings.title: BRONZE SANDCASTLE deploys modified Meterpreter shells (Sophos Counter Threat Unit brief)
findings.summary_md: Sophos CTU and SophosLabs published this brief on 20 Oct 2026 attributing a cluster of incidents to the China-based BRONZE SANDCASTLE group, whose marker is consistent Sandboxie DLL sideloading: legitimate executables such as Start.exe, javaw.exe and bginfo64.exe placed beside malicious sbiedll.dll, jli.dll or snmpapi.dll that read encrypted config.ini payloads. The decrypted payload runs through a custom reflective loader with COFFLoader elements rather than standard Metasploit code, and two versions, 1.1.5 and 1.1.7, were analyzed. Victims spanned the Philippines, Taiwan, Afghanistan, Namibia and likely the Republic of Korea between August 2025 and August 2026. Kaspersky's later ShadowCloud posts cite this brief as covering a fragment of the same campaign and tie shared staging directories to GitDoor.

findings.title: Operation ShadowCloud: initial infection and the GitDoor backdoor (Kaspersky Securelist, Part 1)
findings.summary_md: Kaspersky GReAT researchers Saurabh Sharma and Noushin Shabab posted part 1 of the Operation ShadowCloud analysis at 08:00:37 UTC on 17 Nov 2026, roughly three hours before the Hacker News story that this cluster carries. The post documents two MeshCentral Agent instances (MD5 74b025084026d8d9a64661bf995d835b) inside a Taiwanese organization, hard-coded to wss://27.102.66[.]162:443/agent.ashx and used to drop a sideloading chain of a legitimate binary, a loader DLL and an encrypted config.ini. It details the Type 1 and Type 2 loaders and the GitDoor backdoor, which takes commands from public repository LatonyCharnleyaW/Havo and uploads results to private LatonyCharnleyaW/Trix, with Ably at rest.ably.io as a second channel. Kaspersky says victims were found in Asia and Africa, mainly the government sector, and that Sophos had already touched on a fragment of the campaign.

findings.title: Operation ShadowCloud: GraphDoor backdoor, plug-ins and attribution (Kaspersky Securelist, Part 2)
findings.summary_md: Posted at 08:00:43 UTC on 17 Nov 2026, six seconds after part 1, this second Securelist post covers GraphDoor: it opens a named pipe derived from its own process ID, creates Intel_Log under ProgramData with a GUID-named subdirectory, authenticates to login.microsoftonline.com on port 443 and stages harvested data on the victim SharePoint drive through Microsoft Graph. It lists the plug-ins kl.ts, pr.ts, scr.ts, moveDir.ts, channel.ts, abchannel.ts and ab2channel.ts, the last a covert SOCKS5 proxy tunneling TCP over Ably's Pusher-compatible WebSocket service. Attribution clues point to Chinese-speaking groups: FamousSparrow and CopperTurtle implants shared staging directories with GitDoor within a one-day window, a FamousSparrow RC4 key reappears in the loader set, and Cobalt Strike beacons ran on ms[.]twnic[.]top and ekmt[.]tw alongside GraphDoor proxy C2.
